analysis.notes: A sixteen-bar minor tune that lives on i and its minor ii–V (Bm7b5–E7). The iv chord (Dm7) arrives in bar 7, the relative major (Cmaj7) in bar 13, and the F7–E7 in bar 8 is a tritone-flavoured approach into the dominant. Because so much of the tune sits on Am6, it is the place to learn the minor tonic sounds: m6, m(maj7), and the A minor pentatonic/blues scale. The melody is still under copyright, so learn it by ear from a recording; only the chords are here.

learning.why: Slow, minor, and mostly one chord: room to hear the minor ii–V resolve and to work on tone, phrasing, and space rather than chasing changes.
concepts: Minor ii–V–i at a slow tempo
drills: Comp with a two-feel bass in the guitar (thumb on 1 and 3) under Am6 and E7b9 shapes.
Solo with only the A blues scale for two choruses, then only chord tones for two.
Over every E7, land the G# on beat one and resolve to A.
Play a chorus using no more than three notes per bar.
listen: Ella Fitzgerald and Louis Armstrong — Porgy and Bess (1958)
milestones: Know the form and changes from memory
Comp shells through the form without looking
Comp drop-2 voicings with the trio
Play a chord-tone solo over the whole form
Play the melody from memory (learn it by ear from a recording)
